entries.what: God creates the heavens and the earth (1:1). Genesis gives no date, and Christians differ on how to read the six days.
From Adam to Noah, ten generations (chapter 5), then the flood and God's covenant with every living creature (6 to 9).
The nations spread out, Babel is scattered, and ten generations run from Shem to Abraham (10:1 to 11:26).
Joseph is sold into Egypt, rises to rule under Pharaoh, and brings his family there in a famine (37 to 50).
Jacob's family multiplies in Egypt and is put to forced labor, building the store cities Pithom and Rameses (1:6-14).
Israel arrives at Mount Sinai (19:1), where God gives the Ten Commandments and makes his covenant.
The tabernacle is set up on the first day of the first month of the second year, and God's glory fills it (40:17, 34).

entries.when: The first month of the second year
entries.what: The tabernacle is set up at Sinai on the first day of the month, a year after Israel left Egypt (Exodus 40:17), and the LORD calls to Moses from it (1:1).

entries.when: Seven days, and the eighth day
entries.what: Aaron and his sons are ordained (chapter 8). On the eighth day the glory of the LORD appears and fire burns up the offering (9:23-24). Nadab and Abihu die (10:1-2).
All the words of Leviticus are given at Sinai before the first day of the second month, when Numbers begins (Numbers 1:1).

entries.when: The second year, second month, first day
entries.what: At Sinai, a year after leaving Egypt, the LORD commands the first count of the people (1:1).

entries.when: The second year, second month, twentieth day
entries.what: The cloud lifts from the tabernacle and Israel sets out from Sinai (10:11).
At Kadesh the scouts return after forty days. The people refuse the land and are sentenced to forty years in the wilderness (13:25; 14:34).
The years of wandering, passed over almost in silence. Deuteronomy counts thirty-eight years from Kadesh to the Brook of Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14).

entries.when: The fortieth year, fifth month, first day
entries.what: Aaron dies on Mount Hor, one of the few exact dates in the book (33:38).
Israel camps on the plains of Moab across from Jericho. Balaam blesses, Israel falls at Peor, and the new generation is counted (22:1; 26:63).

entries.when: The fortieth year, eleventh month, first day
entries.what: On the plains of Moab, Moses begins to explain the law to the generation that grew up in the wilderness (1:3-5).
Moses hands leadership to Joshua, writes down the law, and teaches Israel his song (31:7-9; 31:22).
Moses dies on Mount Nebo at 120 years old, in sight of the land. Israel mourns him for thirty days (34:5-8).

entries.when: The tenth day of the first month
entries.what: Israel crosses the Jordan and camps at Gilgal (4:19). Four days later it keeps the Passover in the land (5:10).
Jericho falls, Israel is beaten at Ai and then takes it, and Gibeon wins its treaty (chapters 6 to 9).
The campaigns in the south and the north (11:18). Caleb's ages in 14:7-10 suggest about seven years.
The land is divided by lot at Gilgal and Shiloh, and the cities of refuge are named (chapters 13 to 21).
Joshua, now old, gives his farewell, renews the covenant at Shechem, and dies at the age of 110 (23:1; 24:29).

entries.when: In the days of King Ahab
entries.what: Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two sons, as Joshua's oath had said (6:26; 1 Kings 16:34).
The tribes fight for their land and leave many Canaanite towns standing (chapter 1). A new generation does not know the LORD (2:10).
Cushan-rishathaim rules over Israel. Othniel delivers them, and the land has rest (3:8-11).
Jabin and Sisera oppress Israel. Deborah, Barak and Jael (chapters 4 and 5).
Midian's raids, and Gideon (chapters 6 to 8). Abimelech rules three years after him (9:22).
The Philistines rule over Israel (13:1). Samson judges twenty years in the days of the Philistines (15:20).
The two closing stories. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, serves before the ark, which places the war with Benjamin early in the period (20:28).
Elimelech, Naomi and their sons go to live in Moab (1:1-2).
The sons marry Ruth and Orpah, and all three men die (1:4-5).

entries.when: The start of the barley harvest
entries.what: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem (1:22).

entries.when: Through the barley and wheat harvests
entries.what: Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, a season of perhaps seven weeks (2:23).

entries.when: A night at the end of the harvest
entries.what: Ruth goes to Boaz at the threshing floor (chapter 3).
Boaz settles the matter at the town gate before ten elders (chapter 4).
Ruth bears a son, the grandfather of David (4:13-17).
After the Philistines send it back, the ark stays at Kiriath-jearim (7:2).
David lives in Philistine territory, at Ziklag (27:7).
The Greek translation divides Samuel in two. The best-preserved copy of Samuel later found among the Dead Sea Scrolls often agrees with the Greek against the standard Hebrew.
David takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed, and Nathan confronts him (chapters 11 and 12).

entries.when: Two years, three years, two years
entries.what: Absalom kills Amnon two years after Tamar is raped, stays three years in Geshur, and waits two years in Jerusalem to see the king (13:23, 38; 14:28).
Absalom's revolt (15:7, where the BSB follows some Greek copies and the Syriac; the standard Hebrew has forty).
The Greek translation divides Samuel in two. The best-preserved Samuel scroll among the Dead Sea Scrolls often agrees with the Greek.
Elijah announces the drought, and the contest on Mount Carmel comes ‘in the third year of the drought’ (18:1). The New Testament gives three and a half years (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).
The Greek translation divides Kings in two and sets it with Samuel as the four books of Kingdoms.
The ark is brought to Jerusalem (chapters 13 to 16), and God promises David a house (chapter 17).
The Greek translation divides Chronicles in two.
Job lives in Uz, in a world like that of the patriarchs: wealth in flocks and herds, a father offering sacrifices for his household, no law or temple (1:1-5).
In one day Job loses his flocks, his servants and his ten children, and then his health (1:13-19; 2:7).
Three friends sit with him for seven days in silence, then argue through three rounds of speeches (2:11 to 27:23).
Elihu speaks; then the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind (32:1 to 41:34).
Job prays for his friends, and the LORD restores his fortunes. He lives to see four generations (42:7-17).
Copies and fragments of Job, among them an Aramaic translation, are made; they were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
The five books are gathered into their present shape, most think in the centuries after the return. The exact date is not known.
The Psalms are put into Greek in the Septuagint, with a slightly different numbering and an extra Psalm 151 ‘outside the number’.

entries.when: Before the exile, on one view
entries.what: Some scholars place the finished book in the last years of the kings of Judah.
An Egyptian army comes near and the siege is lifted for a time, but the Egyptians withdraw and the siege resumes (Jeremiah 37:5-11; compare 4:17).
The people fast and mourn for the city in the fifth and seventh months (Zechariah 7:5). Chapter 5, with the ruins overgrown, may come from these years.
Jewish scholars translate the Scriptures into Greek. The Septuagint opens Lamentations with a preface naming Jeremiah as the weeping poet.
Daniel remains in service until then (1:21). His last vision is dated to Cyrus's third year (10:1).
Edomites settle in southern Judah, later called Idumea. Malachi speaks of Edom's land lying waste (Malachi 1:2-4).
The risen Jesus is carried up into heaven near Bethany (24:50-51; Acts 1:3).
John baptizes at Bethany beyond the Jordan and points to Jesus: ‘the Lamb of God’ (1:28-29).
Jesus clears the temple in Jerusalem and talks with Nicodemus at night (2:13 to 3:21).
At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus heals a man ill for thirty-eight years (5:1-9).
Near the lake, Jesus feeds five thousand and calls himself the bread of life (6:4, 6:35).
At the harvest feast Jesus offers living water and calls himself the light of the world (7:2, 7:37, 8:12).
In the temple Jesus says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (10:22-30).
Lazarus raised; the last supper; the cross on the day of Preparation; the empty tomb (11:55, 19:14, 20:1).
The risen Jesus meets his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias and restores Peter (21:1-19).
Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, teaches in Corinth and helps the believers (Acts 18:27-28). Paul later writes, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it” (3:6).
Paul writes an earlier letter to Corinth, now lost (5:9).
Paul writes an earlier letter to Corinth, now lost (1 Corinthians 5:9).
A painful visit to Corinth (2:1), not told in Acts. Paul will later call his next visit the third (13:1).
Paul writes a letter “through many tears” (2:4), and sends Titus to Corinth. Many think the letter is lost; some think part of it is 2 Corinthians 10 to 13.
A crushing time of danger in the province of Asia, when Paul felt he was under “the sentence of death” (1:9). What it was is not known.
Paul waits for Titus at Troas, then goes on to Macedonia, where Titus meets him with good news (2:12-13; 7:5-7).
Peter draws back from eating with Gentile believers at Antioch, and Paul opposes him to his face (2:11-14).
Paul's ship, carrying him as a prisoner, shelters at Fair Havens on Crete's south coast (Acts 27:7-13).
Titus goes to Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast (2 Timothy 4:10).
Melchizedek, king of Salem, blesses Abraham, and Abraham gives him a tenth (Genesis 14:18-20; Hebrews 7:1-2).
God makes his covenant with Israel at Sinai and gives the pattern of the tabernacle (Exodus 19 to 25; Hebrews 8:5).
God counts Abram's faith as righteousness (Genesis 15:6); years later Abraham offers Isaac (Genesis 22). James joins the two (2:21-23).
Rahab hides Israel's spies at Jericho and is spared (Joshua 2; 6:25). James names her beside Abraham (2:25).
Elijah prays, and there is no rain, and then rain again (1 Kings 17 to 18; James 5:17-18).
His brothers do not believe in him (John 7:5).
The risen Jesus appears to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), who becomes a leader of the church in Jerusalem.
God waits patiently while the ark is built; eight people are saved through water (Genesis 6 to 8; 1 Peter 3:20).
Israel is redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the Passover lamb and called a kingdom of priests at Sinai (Exodus 12; 19:6).
Peter preaches in Jerusalem; among the hearers are people from Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia (Acts 2:9).
God brings the flood and keeps Noah and his household, eight people (Genesis 6 to 8; 2 Peter 2:5).
Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed and Lot is rescued (Genesis 19; 2 Peter 2:6-7).
Balaam son of Beor is hired to curse Israel and is rebuked by his donkey (Numbers 22; 2 Peter 2:15-16).
Peter, James and John see Jesus transfigured on a mountain (Mark 9:2-8; 2 Peter 1:16-18).
The first witnesses hear, see and touch ‘the Word of life’ (1:1-3; John 1:14).
Jesus gives the new command: ‘Love one another’ (John 13:34).
Jesus says, ‘whoever receives the one I send receives Me’ (John 13:20).
God's judgment and the sons of God in Genesis 6, read by many as the angels of verse 6.
Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed (Genesis 19; Jude 7).
Israel leaves Egypt; the unbelieving die in the wilderness; Balaam and Korah (Numbers 14, 16, 22).
The writings later gathered as 1 Enoch are composed; Aramaic fragments are found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Ritual texts from Ebla in Syria describe a goat driven out into the wasteland in a rite of cleansing, an early parallel to the goat of chapter 16.
Abraham leaves Ur and Haran for Canaan (11:31 to 12:9). Many readers place him early in the second millennium BC; others think the stories cannot be dated.
Isaac, the son of promise, and Jacob, who is renamed Israel and has twelve sons (21 to 35).
Texts from Mari in Syria describe the mustering of tribal groups for military service, as the census of chapter 1 does.
The Laws of Hammurabi are carved in Babylon, with rules for a slave woman who bears children for a wife, as Hagar does for Sarah.
The Code of Hammurabi in Babylon sends a wife accused by others to the river ordeal, in which an innocent woman could drown. The rite of Numbers 5 uses nothing that could harm.
The oldest fairly complete copy of the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, with its story of humans made from clay and a great flood.
The Hyksos, foreign rulers of northern Egypt for about a century, are driven out. Some scholars link the new king who did not know Joseph with the distrust of foreigners that followed.
The last great walled city at Jericho is destroyed, on the date Kathleen Kenyon gave and most archaeologists hold.
The Nuzi tablets are written in northern Mesopotamia. Scholars once leaned on them to explain the patriarchs' customs; they now use them with caution.
On the traditional view, Moses writes the Torah in the time of the exodus. The date depends on when the exodus happened, which is debated.

entries.when: About 1446 BC, on the early date
entries.what: Israel leaves Egypt, counting back 480 years from Solomon's fourth year (1 Kings 6:1). Thutmose III or Amenhotep II would be the Pharaoh.
The two main dates proposed for the exodus. The wilderness years follow whichever is right.
The two main dates proposed for the exodus. The last words of Moses come forty years after whichever is right.
The two main dates proposed for Israel's entry into Canaan. Which is right depends on the date of the exodus.

entries.when: The fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC
entries.what: Hittite great kings make treaties with lesser kings: history, requirements, witnesses, blessings and curses. Many scholars compare the shape of Deuteronomy with them.
An Egyptian list at Soleb in Nubia, under Amenhotep III, names a land of the Shasu of Yhw, the earliest known name outside the Bible that looks like YHWH.
The Amarna letters, clay tablets found in Egypt: the kings of Canaan's small city-states write to Pharaoh, a ruler of Jerusalem and a king of Hazor among them.

entries.when: About 1375 to 1050 BC, or about 1200 to 1050 BC
entries.what: The two main spans proposed for the judges. Which is right depends on the date of the exodus.
The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope is written, an official's advice to his son in thirty chapters, close to Proverbs 22:17 to 23:11.
Egyptian love songs are written on papyri and pottery, in which lovers call each other brother and sister and praise each other, as the Song does.
Israel leaves Egypt, on the view that places the exodus under Ramesses II and reads the 480 years as a round number.
Hazor, the largest city in Canaan, is destroyed by a great fire. Who burned it is argued.
Ramesses II reigns. Many identify his Delta capital, Pi-Ramesses, with the store city Rameses (1:11).
Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast name offerings with words close to the Hebrew ones.
An Egyptian stone of King Merneptah names Israel as a people: the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.
Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stone names Israel as a people already in Canaan, the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.
The monument of Pharaoh Merneptah names a people called Israel already living in Canaan.
The monument of Pharaoh Merneptah names a people called Israel living in Canaan.
Many new villages appear in the hill country of Canaan, part of the case made for the later date.
The great powers of the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Egypt's hold on Canaan weakens.
More than 250 small villages appear in the central hill country, most of them on hilltops.
Poems from Ugarit on the Syrian coast tell of Litan, a twisting sea serpent defeated by Baal or his sister Anat, a figure like the Leviathan of Job 3 and 41.
The Philistines settle on the southern coast. Reliefs of Ramesses III name the Peleset among the Sea Peoples.
The Song of Deborah, widely held to be one of the oldest Hebrew poems, perhaps composed not long after the battle (chapter 5).
The days when the judges ruled, the period in which the story is set (1:1).
The Philistines settle on the southern coastal plain, part of the movement that Egyptian records call the Sea Peoples.
Samuel is born to Hannah and given to the LORD at Shiloh in the last years of Eli (chapters 1 to 3).
Saul's reign, on most estimates. The Hebrew of 13:1 is damaged, and Acts 13:21 gives him forty years.

entries.when: Late in the eleventh century BC
entries.what: The elders ask Samuel for a king like all the other nations (chapter 8).
Samuel anoints David at Bethlehem while Saul still reigns (chapter 16).
Saul and three of his sons die on Mount Gilboa (chapter 31). The date is the usual one, and Saul's dates are uncertain.
Saul and three of his sons die on Mount Gilboa, and David, at Ziklag, sings his lament (chapter 1).
David reigns over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months (2:11). Saul's son Ish-bosheth reigns over the north for two years (2:10).
Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa (chapter 10). Saul's dates are uncertain.
David reigns at Hebron, over Judah alone. Chronicles mentions the years only in passing (3:4; 29:27).
All Israel anoints David king at Hebron, and he takes Jerusalem (chapter 5). The dates are approximate.
All Israel anoints David at Hebron, and he takes Jerusalem (chapter 11). The dates are approximate.
The Gezer tablet, a small limestone tablet found in 1908, lists the farming months of the year in an order like that of the feasts.
Egypt is weak and Assyria not yet pressing west. David subdues the small kingdoms around Israel (chapter 8).
David reigns in Jerusalem, by the usual dating. Seventy-three psalms are linked with him by their headings; what ‘of David’ means is debated.
Solomon builds the temple on Zion (1 Kings 6), by the usual dating. Many psalms belong to its worship and its singers.
Some sayings may go back to Solomon's day. Proverbs pass from mouth to mouth for generations before they are written.

entries.when: The tenth century BC, on one view
entries.what: If Solomon wrote the book, as Jewish and Christian tradition held and some conservative scholars still argue, it comes from his reign.

entries.when: The tenth century BC, on one view
entries.what: If Solomon wrote the Song, or it comes from his court, it dates from his reign.

entries.when: The 900s BC or later, or the 400s to 300s BC
entries.what: The two main dates proposed for the writing of the book.
Some date the writing of Job to the time of Solomon, when Israel's wisdom writing flourished.
David dies, after forty years as king (5:4), and Solomon reigns (1 Kings 2).
David dies after forty years as king, and Solomon secures the throne (chapters 1 and 2).
David dies after forty years as king, and Solomon reigns (29:26-28).
Solomon begins to reign, and asks God for wisdom at Gibeon (chapter 1). The dates are approximate.
Solomon reigns. He asks God for wisdom, and he composes three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 3; 4:32).
Solomon reigns in Jerusalem, famed for wisdom, wealth and building. The Teacher of chapters 1 and 2 speaks in his voice.
Solomon reigns. He is remembered for a thousand and five songs and for his knowledge of plants and animals (1 Kings 4:32-33).
Solomon begins the temple in his fourth year, ‘in the four hundred and eightieth year’ after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1).
In Solomon's fourth year the building of the temple begins, dated 480 years after the exodus (6:1).
Solomon begins the temple, on the traditional dating from 1 Kings 6:1.
The temple is finished after seven years (6:38) and dedicated at the autumn feast (chapter 8). Readers differ on whether the dedication came that year or the next.
Shoshenq I, the Bible's Shishak, reigns in Egypt. Jeroboam flees to him from Solomon (11:40).
At Solomon's death the kingdom splits. Judah, in the south, keeps David's line of kings.
Solomon dies after forty years (11:42), and the kingdom divides at Shechem (chapter 12). Other reckonings give 927 or 922 BC.
Solomon dies, and the kingdom divides under Rehoboam (chapter 10).
The kingdom divides. Jeroboam I becomes king of the north and sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12).
The kingdom divides. Jeroboam I sets up a golden calf at Bethel (1 Kings 12), the shrine Amos speaks against.
The note that Ziklag still belongs ‘to the kings of Judah’ (27:6) assumes the divided kingdom, so the book was finished after the split.
In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak carries off the treasures of the temple and palace (14:25-26), and lists the places he claims on a wall at Karnak.
Shishak of Egypt invades Judah (chapter 12).
Domesticated camels appear in the Aravah valley, according to a 2013 study, part of the debate over the camels in Genesis.
Asa reigns in Judah, removes the idols, and his heart is fully devoted to the LORD (15:9-24).
Asa reigns forty-one years (chapters 14 to 16).
Baasha kills Jeroboam's son Nadab and wipes out Jeroboam's house, as Ahijah had said (15:27-30).
Mesha, king of Moab, sets up an inscription crediting his god Chemosh with victories over Israel. It names towns that appear in Numbers 21. It was found at Dhiban in 1868.
The Mesha Stele, a Moabite king's inscription, names Chemosh, the god of Moab.

entries.when: The second half of the 800s BC
entries.what: An Aramaic inscription at Tel Dan, most likely set up by Hazael of Damascus, names a king of the house of David.

entries.when: The second half of the 800s BC
entries.what: An Aramaic inscription at Tel Dan, most likely set up by Hazael of Damascus, names a king of the house of David.
Zimri reigns seven days; Omri takes the throne after a civil war and later builds Samaria (16:9-24).
Tirzah is still a royal city of the northern kingdom; Omri reigns there before building Samaria (1 Kings 16:23-24). The Song names Tirzah beside Jerusalem (6:4).
Ahab begins to reign. He marries Jezebel of Sidon and builds a temple for Baal in Samaria (16:29-33). Albright's reckoning gives 869.
Shalmaneser III of Assyria fights a coalition of western kings at Qarqar. His Kurkh Monolith lists Ahab with a large force of chariots.
Ahab dies in battle at Ramoth-gilead (22:34-37), and his son Ahaziah reigns in Israel (22:51).
Ahaziah of Israel dies after his fall, as Elijah had said (1:17), and his brother Joram reigns.
Joram reigns in Israel, and Elisha's ministry fills chapters 3 to 8. Moab rebels (chapter 3), and Mesha tells his side on a stone found at Dhiban in 1868.
Jehoram reigns alone in Judah. Edom rebels, and Philistines and Arabs plunder Jerusalem (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17). A minority of scholars date Obadiah here.
Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah and takes Israel's throne (chapter 9). Albright's reckoning gives 842. The same year Jehu, or his envoy, brings tribute to Shalmaneser III, shown on the Black Obelisk.
Athaliah rules Judah, until the priest Jehoiada crowns Joash in the temple (chapter 11).
Athaliah holds the throne; the infant Joash is hidden in the temple (chapters 22 and 23).
Jehu kills Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel and Ahab's house at Jezreel (2 Kings 9 to 10): ‘the bloodshed of Jezreel’ of 1:4.
Mesha, king of Moab, records on his monument that he devoted an Israelite town to his god, using the same word Deuteronomy uses for the ban.
Mesha, king of Moab, records on his monument that he devoted an Israelite town to his god, using the word Joshua uses for the ban.
Mesha king of Moab sets up a stone at Dibon naming Omri as a king of Israel who oppressed Moab. It was found in 1868.
Joash reigns. After Jehoiada dies, Zechariah is stoned in the temple court (24:20-22).
Joash reigns in Judah, at first under the priest Jehoiada's guidance (2 Kings 11 to 12). Those who date Joel early, in the ninth century, often place it here.
An inscription on a plastered wall at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor. It was found in 1967.
Jehoash reigns in Israel. Elisha dies in his reign, after the arrows of victory (13:14-20).
Jeroboam II restores Israel's borders, as Jonah had said (14:25). Amos and Hosea preach in the north.
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel, a time of wider borders and wealth. Hosea begins in his reign (1:1).
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel and pushes its borders north and east (2 Kings 14:25).
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel. Jonah son of Amittai speaks the word that Israel's border will be restored (2 Kings 14:25). The guide to the kings places his ministry within these years.
Uzziah reigns in Judah, first beside his father Amaziah, alone from 767.
Uzziah reigns, and his skin disease makes his son Jotham regent (chapter 26).
Amos, a man from Judah, preaches at Bethel under Jeroboam II.
Amos preaches at Bethel, ‘two years before the earthquake’ (1:1). His ministry may have lasted a season or a year.
A strong earthquake. The guide to the kings dates traces at Hazor and other sites to about 760; the book's introduction says the link to Amos is probable but not certain.
Hosea begins to preach. The site's guide to the kings has him speaking to about 715 BC; the book's introduction gives about 755 to about 725.
Jeroboam's son Zechariah reigns six months and is murdered. Jehu's line ends, as 1:4 warned (2 Kings 15:8-12).
Menahem reigns and pays Assyria a heavy tribute (2 Kings 15:19-20).
Jotham reigns in Judah, first as regent for Uzziah. Micah's heading names him (1:1).
Tiglath-pileser III, called Pul (15:19), rules Assyria and begins deporting conquered peoples. Menahem pays him tribute.
Tiglath-pileser III makes Assyria an empire of conquest and deportation.
Tiglath-pileser III begins to rule Assyria and turns west.
Tiglath-pileser III comes to the throne of Assyria and turns west.
In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord on his throne and is sent (6:1-8).
Micah preaches, by the book's introduction. The site's guide to the kings gives 735 to 700.
Aram and Israel attack Judah. Isaiah meets Ahaz and gives the sign of Immanuel (chapter 7). Ahaz appeals to Assyria.
Ahaz reigns in Judah and turns to Assyria for help (2 Kings 16).
Aram and Israel attack Judah; Ahaz appeals to Assyria, which takes Damascus and Galilee (15:29; 16:5-9).
Israel and Damascus fight Judah and Assyria. Many scholars connect 5:8-15 with this war. Galilee and Gilead are lost.
The Assyrian deportations from northern Israel begin, which many take to be ‘the captivity of the land’ in 18:30.
Assyria takes Damascus; Galilee and Gilead are annexed, within the few years 7:16 allows.
Hoshea, the last king of Israel, comes to the throne. He later stops paying tribute and turns to Egypt (2 Kings 17:4).
Samaria falls after a three-year siege (17:5-6). Most histories give 722 or 721. Sargon II claimed the capture and the deportation.
Samaria falls to Assyria, as Ahijah had warned (14:15-16), and Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple, as the LORD had warned Solomon (9:6-9).
Samaria falls to Assyria, which settles other peoples in the north (2 Kings 17:24). Their descendants are among the neighbors of Ezra 4.
Samaria falls and the northern kingdom ends. The site's guide to the kings gives 723 or 722, and most histories 722 or 721.
Samaria falls after a three-year siege, and much of its people is deported (2 Kings 17:5-6). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Hosea's words are carried south and kept in Judah, where most scholars think the book took its final form.
Samaria falls, about a generation after Amos (2 Kings 17). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Assyria takes Samaria and ends the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Samaria falls to Assyria, as Micah warned (1:6). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Hezekiah reigns in Judah, removes the high places and rebels against Assyria (chapter 18). Galil's reckoning gives 726 to 697.
Hezekiah reigns, reopens the temple and keeps the Passover (chapters 29 to 32).
Hezekiah reigns in Judah, by Thiele's reckoning in the site's guide. Galil's reckoning gives 726 to 697.
Hezekiah becomes king of Judah, the last king named in Hosea's heading (1:1).
Hezekiah reigns in Judah and, Jeremiah 26:18-19 says, heeds Micah's warning.
Hezekiah reigns in Judah. His men copy further proverbs of Solomon, now chapters 25 to 29 (25:1).
Sennacherib invades Judah, takes Lachish and besieges Jerusalem, but does not take it (chapters 18 and 19).
Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah (chapter 32).
Sennacherib invades Judah and besieges Jerusalem, which is spared (chapters 36 and 37). His annals claim forty-six fortified cities.
Sennacherib invades Judah, takes Lachish and besieges Jerusalem, which is spared (2 Kings 18 to 19).
Sennacherib invades Judah and besieges Jerusalem (2 Kings 18 to 19). His palace at Nineveh shows the siege of Lachish.
On the traditional view, the book is substantially complete, with chapters 40 to 66 looking ahead.
Nineveh becomes Assyria's royal capital under Sennacherib.
The library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh holds copies of Enuma Elish and of the Gilgamesh flood tablet.
Others place the writing in the seventh century BC.
Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, at first beside his father (21:1).
Manasseh reigns, the longest reign in Judah (chapter 33).
Manasseh reigns in Judah as an Assyrian vassal.
Manasseh reigns in Judah as an Assyrian vassal, the low point of Judah's worship (2 Kings 21).
The Assyrian king Esarhaddon binds his subjects by a treaty that commands them to love his heir. Its curses are often compared with chapter 28.
Ashurbanipal of Assyria sacks Thebes in Egypt, which Nahum names as past (3:8-10).
Nahum speaks, probably in Josiah's reign by the site's guide to the kings; some scholars prefer soon after 663, others near 612.
Josiah reigns; he dies at Megiddo fighting Pharaoh Neco (chapters 34 and 35).
Josiah reigns, from the age of eight. Zephaniah's heading names him (1:1).
Josiah reigns in Judah and burns bones on the altar at Bethel, as the man of God from Judah had said (13:2; 2 Kings 23:15-16).
Ashurbanipal dies, as scholars date it, and Assyria weakens quickly.
Most scholars place Zephaniah here, before or early in the reform; the guide to the kings gives the span of Josiah's reign.
Josiah's twelfth year, when 2 Chronicles 34 begins his reform.
Nabopolassar founds the Neo-Babylonian kingdom.
The final edition of the book, on the view that it belongs to one history running from Deuteronomy to Kings.
The final edition of the book, on the view that it belongs to one history running from Deuteronomy to Kings.
Jeremiah prophesies in Judah and promises a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:8-12).
In the reign of King Josiah the Book of the Law is found in the temple, and the king reforms the worship of Judah (2 Kings 22 and 23).
In Josiah's eighteenth year the Book of the Law is found in the temple (22:3-8).
Josiah's eighteenth year: the Book of the Law found and the covenant renewed (2 Kings 22 to 23).
Nineveh, Assyria's capital, falls to the Babylonians and Medes.
Nineveh is destroyed by the Babylonians and the Medes. Nahum announced its fall.
Babylonians and Medes destroy Nineveh, as the Babylonian Chronicle records.
Nineveh falls to the Babylonians and Medes.
Nineveh falls, as Zephaniah 2:13 foretold.
Josiah is killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Neco (23:29).
Assyria's last stand at Harran collapses (609); Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish (605).
Josiah is killed at Megiddo; Jehoiakim later takes the throne (2 Kings 23:29-34).
Many scholars, and the site's guide to the kings, place Habakkuk in Jehoiakim's reign. Others place him late in Josiah's reign.
Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish, and Judah becomes Babylon's vassal (24:1).
Nebuchadnezzar II, as crown prince, defeats Egypt at Carchemish and takes control of Judah. He reigns over Babylon until 562 BC.
Nebuchadnezzar, as crown prince, defeats Egypt at Carchemish and becomes king of Babylon. By Daniel's account, Daniel and his friends are taken that year (1:1-6).
Nebuchadnezzar II reigns over Babylon. The stories of chapters 1 to 4 are set in his court.
Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish, and Nebuchadnezzar becomes king.
Two small silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem carry a form of the priests' blessing of Numbers 6.
Ezekiel, a priest in exile, draws on the language of Leviticus and restates its rules for priests in his vision of a new temple (Ezekiel 44).
Two small silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem carry a form of the priests' blessing of 6:24-26. They were found in 1979.

entries.when: The 500s to 300s BC, on a third view
entries.what: Others date the writing after the Babylonian exile, often arguing from the book's language.
Babylon takes the people of Judah into exile. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, and some exiles return.
Jerusalem surrenders; Jehoiachin and thousands are carried to Babylon (24:10-16). The Babylonian Chronicle records it.
Ezekiel, among the exiles, names Job with Noah and Daniel as righteous men of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20).
After Jehoiakim's rebellion, Jerusalem surrenders. King Jehoiachin and many leaders and craftsmen are taken to Babylon, and Zedekiah is made king.
A larger deportation takes King Jehoiachin and many others to Babylon, among them the prophet Ezekiel.
Babylon takes Jerusalem and carries off King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24).
Zedekiah rebels, trusting in Egypt, and the Babylonian army begins a siege of Jerusalem that lasts about a year and a half.
Jerusalem falls to Babylon and Judah goes into exile. 2 Chronicles 36:21 says the land then enjoyed its Sabbaths, echoing 26:34-35.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem, and no descendant of David rules again. Psalm 89 holds the promise of chapter 7 up to God.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. Judah goes into exile ‘because of their unfaithfulness’ (9:1).
Babylon burns the temple and Jerusalem (chapter 36).
The Babylonians burn Jerusalem and its temple and carry the people of Judah into exile (2 Kings 25).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple and carries many into exile. Psalm 137 remembers weeping ‘by the rivers of Babylon’.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. The second half of the book speaks to the exiles.

The vivid detail of chapters 2 and 4 suggests they were written within a few years of the fall.
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed. The temple vessels Belshazzar later drinks from were carried to Babylon (5:2-3).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem, and Zion is plowed like a field (2 Kings 25).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple (2 Kings 25).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem: the Day of the LORD on the city (2 Kings 25).
The Babylonians destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and carries Judah into exile.
Jerusalem and the temple are burned (25:8-10). Many historians prefer 587.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple, and many of Judah's people are scattered (2 Kings 25). Joel 3:2 speaks of a people scattered among the nations.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple; many historians prefer 587. Edom sides with the conqueror (Psalm 137:7).
Most scholars, and the site's guide to the kings, place Obadiah here.
The finished book of Kings, whose last scene is Jehoiachin's release in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27-30).
Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison (25:27-30). The finished book of Kings can be no earlier.
Nabonidus, Babylon's last king, spends about ten years at Tayma and leaves his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon (chapter 5).
On the multiple-author view, chapters 40 to 55 come from these last years of the exile, as Cyrus rises.
Many critical scholars date the final shaping of Genesis and the Torah to the Persian period, after the exile.
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon.
Cyrus of Persia decrees the return (36:22-23).
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, almost without a fight.
Cyrus takes Babylon, and the next year the first exiles go home (Ezra 1).
Cyrus lets the exiles go home. Many stay in Babylonia and Persia (Ezra 1).
Persia takes Babylon, and exiles may return home (Ezra 1). Psalm 126 sings of the LORD restoring Zion's captives.
Cyrus takes Babylon and lets the exiles go home, as 44:28 and 45:1 speak of him.
Cyrus takes Babylon and allows the exiles to return. The poems show no knowledge of the return, so most scholars date the collection before it.
Babylon falls to Cyrus of Persia. In Daniel, Belshazzar is killed and ‘Darius the Mede’ receives the kingdom (5:30-31).
Cyrus of Persia conquers Babylon and soon allows the exiles to return and rebuild (Ezra 1).
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon and soon lets the exiles return (Ezra 1).
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, and the exiles begin to return.
Cyrus decrees the return, the event with which Chronicles ends (2 Chronicles 36:22-23).
In his first year over Babylon, Cyrus decrees that the house of the LORD be rebuilt, and the first exiles go home (chapters 1 and 2).
The altar is rebuilt in the seventh month, and the Feast of Tabernacles is kept (3:1-6).
The temple's foundation is laid, with shouts of joy and loud weeping (3:8-13).
Opposition and discouragement; the work on the temple stands still (4:4-5, 24).
The returned exiles rebuild the altar and lay the temple's foundation; then the work stops (Ezra 3 to 4).
The altar rebuilt and the foundations laid; then the work stops for about sixteen years (Ezra 3 to 4).
The first gold darics are struck under Darius I (29:7).

entries.when: Late sixth or early fifth century BC
entries.what: On the multiple-author view, chapters 56 to 66 address the community after the return.
Darius I takes the Persian throne and spends his first years putting down revolts.
Darius I takes the Persian throne amid revolts, recorded at Behistun.
Darius I seizes the Persian throne amid revolts.
Zerubbabel, of David's line, leads the returned community (3:19).
Haggai and Zechariah urge the builders on, and the work begins again in Darius's second year (5:1-2; Haggai 1:1, 15).
Darius I has his deeds carved into the rock at Behistun, the kind of lasting record Job wishes his words could have (19:23-24).
Haggai's first message; the work begins twenty-four days later (1:1, 15).
The second message, at the Feast of Tabernacles (2:1).
The third and fourth messages, on one day (2:10, 20).
Zechariah's first word, in Darius's second year (1:1), soon after Haggai began.
The eight night visions (1:7).
The question from Bethel about fasting (7:1).
The rebuilt temple is finished.
The rebuilt temple is dedicated.

The second temple is finished in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:15).
The temple is finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15).
The temple is finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15).
The rebuilt temple is finished (Ezra 6:15).
The prophet Malachi rebukes priests who offer blind and lame animals, which Leviticus 22 forbids (Malachi 1:8).
An Aramaic papyrus of the Words of Ahiqar is copied at Elephantine in Egypt: a sage's sayings and story, with parallels to proverbs on discipline and speech.

Many modern scholars place Joel here, after the exile, with the temple rebuilt and elders and priests leading. The site's guide to the kings calls the date disputed, from the ninth century to the Persian period.

entries.when: The 400s or 300s BC, on another view
entries.what: Many place the book's final editing after the exile, in the Persian period, often with chapters 1 to 9 among the last parts.

entries.when: The 400s to 200s BC, on another view
entries.what: Many modern scholars date the Song's final form to the Persian or early Greek period, pointing to its Hebrew.
Xerxes I reigns. An accusation is lodged against Judah (4:6), and the story of Esther takes place in his court.
Xerxes I, the Ahasuerus of the book, reigns over Persia.
The king's feast in his third year, and Vashti's refusal (1:3, 12).
Xerxes' invasion of Greece ends in defeat at Salamis and Plataea. The book does not mention it.
Esther is taken to the king in the tenth month of his seventh year and made queen (2:16-17).
In the first month of the twelfth year, the lot is cast and Haman's decree goes out (3:7, 12).
Mordecai's decree lets the Jews defend themselves (8:9).
The thirteenth of Adar: the day of destruction is overturned (9:1).
Most scholars date Malachi to the middle of the fifth century BC; the book gives no date.
Artaxerxes I reigns. His officials persuade him to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (4:7-23).
Artaxerxes I reigns over Persia. His officials have the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls stopped (Ezra 4:7-23).
Xerxes is killed in a plot at his own court.
Artaxerxes the First reigns over Persia.
Ezra and then Nehemiah come to Jerusalem, on the traditional dating.
Ezra comes from Babylon in Artaxerxes' seventh year (7:7-9). In the ninth month the assembly meets in the rain over the marriages (10:9).
Ezra comes to Jerusalem with a second group of exiles (Ezra 7:7-9).
Ezra goes to Jerusalem, on the traditional dating (Ezra 7).
Ezra comes to Jerusalem.

entries.when: About 450 to 250 BC, on another view
entries.what: Most modern scholars place the book in the Persian or early Greek period, mainly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords.
In the month of Chislev, in Susa, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's wall is broken down (1:1-3).
Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem as governor in Artaxerxes' twentieth year (Nehemiah 2:1).
In Nisan of the king's twentieth year, Nehemiah asks Artaxerxes for leave to rebuild (2:1-8).
The wall is finished in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul (6:15).

entries.when: Autumn 445 BC, if the chapters follow in order
entries.what: Ezra reads the law, the Feast of Tabernacles is kept, the people confess, and the pledge is sealed (chapters 8 to 10).
Nehemiah's first term as governor of Judah, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes (5:14).
Nehemiah becomes governor and rebuilds the walls.
Nehemiah goes back to the king (13:6).

entries.when: Some time later, about 430 BC on one reckoning
entries.what: Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem and finds the pledges broken (13:6-31). The book does not say how long he was away.
Darius II reigns, possibly the ‘Darius the Persian’ of 12:22, though some think of Darius III.
A letter to the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt gives the dates for the festival of unleavened bread, the earliest evidence of Passover outside the Bible.
Jews at Elephantine in Egypt write to the governor of Judah. Their letter names a high priest Johanan in Jerusalem, a clue in the debate over Ezra's date.
The Jews at Elephantine in Egypt write to the governor of Judah, naming the sons of Sanballat and the high priest Johanan.
Chronicles is written, on the most common dating. Some argue for about 520 to 515 BC, others for about 300 BC.
Chronicles is written, on the most common dating. Some argue for about 520 to 500 BC, others for after Alexander the Great.
Ezra and Nehemiah, one book, reach their final form. Their lists of priests run to Jaddua (Nehemiah 12:11, 22).
Ezra and Nehemiah, one book, reach their final form; the priestly lists run to Jaddua (12:11, 22).

entries.when: The fourth century BC, or later
entries.what: The book is written, in the late Persian period on many views, or in the third or second century BC on others.
If the king of 7:7 was Artaxerxes II, Ezra came in this year, after Nehemiah.
Some scholars place Ezra's arrival here, after Nehemiah.
Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire and dies at Babylon. His empire divides, as the goat's great horn is broken and four grow up (8:8, 21-22).
Cassander founds Thessalonica and names it after his wife, Alexander the Great's half-sister.
The Torah is translated into Greek for Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt, the first part of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.
The Torah is translated into Greek for Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt, the first part of the Septuagint.
Papyri from the archive of Zenon name a local magnate, Tobias, probably of the family of Nehemiah's opponent Tobiah.
The Nash Papyrus, a Hebrew sheet from Egypt, gives the Ten Commandments followed by the Shema.
In the Maccabean revolt the priest Mattathias is compared to Phinehas for his zeal (1 Maccabees 2:26).

entries.when: The second or first century BC
entries.what: The Nash Papyrus, a single Hebrew sheet from Egypt, holds the Ten Commandments followed by the Shema. Tefillin were also found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran.
Second Maccabees calls the fourteenth of Adar Mordecai's day: Purim is known in Judea.
Copies of Ecclesiastes are made that were later found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, ruling out the very latest proposed dates.
The Great Isaiah Scroll is copied, later found at Qumran: all sixty-six chapters as one book.
The Seleucid Antiochus III wins Judea from the Ptolemies at the battle of Panium. Chapter 11 traces the wars of the kings of the north and south.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes reigns. About 171 BC the high priest Onias III is murdered, whom the critical reading takes as the anointed one cut off (9:26).
Antiochus IV tries to suppress Jewish practice in Judea. The books of Maccabees tell of Jews who die sooner than eat pork.
Antiochus desecrates the temple and bans Jewish worship, recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:54. Many read 11:31 of this.
The critical view dates the visions in their final form here; the traditional view places the book in the sixth century BC. Readers differ.
The Greek king Antiochus IV sets up a pagan altar in the temple in Jerusalem, remembered as the abomination of desolation (Daniel 11:31).
The temple of Ezra 6, desecrated under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, is rededicated, the origin of Hanukkah.
Judas Maccabeus retakes and rededicates the temple, remembered at Hanukkah. Antiochus dies the same year.
The temple is cleansed and dedicated again after a Greek king defiled it. Jews remember it at the Feast of Dedication, Hanukkah (10:22).
Rome makes Macedonia a province, and Thessalonica becomes its capital.
The Romans destroy the old Greek city of Corinth. It lies mostly empty for about a century.
The oldest copy of Daniel found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran probably comes from about this time.
A Greek version of Esther with six long additions, including prayers that name God, is in circulation.
Julius Caesar founds Corinth again as a Roman colony. It becomes the seat of the governor of Achaia.
On the plain outside Philippi, Mark Antony and Octavian defeat the killers of Julius Caesar. Soldiers are settled in the city.
Thessalonica takes the winning side in Rome's civil war and is made a free city with its own officials.
Herod the Great becomes king of Judea under Rome. He rules until his death.
Herod the Great rules Judea as king under Rome. Luke begins ‘in the time of Herod king of Judea’ (1:5).
After Octavian's victory at Actium, more settlers come, and Philippi is made a Roman colony.
Octavian, later the emperor Augustus, wins the sea battle of Actium and founds Nicopolis nearby to mark it.
Pergamum receives the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Roma.
Augustus is the first Roman emperor. Luke names his decree for a census (2:1).
A Dead Sea Scrolls text, 4QFlorilegium, reads 7:10-14 of the Branch of David to come.
Cities in the province of Asia call Augustus's birthday the beginning of good news for the world.
When some date the writing of the book: those who think Jonah, or someone near him, wrote it.
Other scholars place Joel here, close to the Babylonian crisis.
When some other scholars date the writing of the book.
The Babylonian king Nabonidus campaigns in Edom's region. In time Arab peoples, at last the Nabateans, take over its heartland.
Jesus is born in Bethlehem, ‘during the time of King Herod’ (2:1). The Magi come; the family flees to Egypt (Matthew 2).
When many scholars date the writing of the book, after the exile.
When chapters 9 to 14 are dated: by Zechariah later in life, or by later prophets; some read chapter 9 against Alexander's conquests of 333 and 332 BC.
Herod dies (some scholars argue for 1 BC). His son Archelaus rules Judea and his son Herod Antipas rules Galilee.
Herod the Great dies. His son Herod Antipas begins to rule Galilee, where most of Mark happens (until AD 39).
Jesus is born in Bethlehem, while Herod is still alive (1:5, 2:4-7).
Herod Antipas rules Galilee. He imprisons John and questions Jesus (3:19-20, 23:7-12).
Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, rules Galilee and the land beyond the Jordan.
Jesus answers the tempter three times from Deuteronomy and names the Shema the most important commandment (Matthew 4:1-11; Mark 12:29-30).
Matthew names Rahab in the family line of Jesus. Hebrews praises her faith and speaks of a rest that Joshua did not give.
Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32).
Matthew names Ruth in the family line of Jesus, and Luke names Boaz (Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32).
Mary's song echoes Hannah's (Luke 1:46-55), and Paul gives Saul forty years (Acts 13:21).
The New Testament reads the promise of chapter 7 of Jesus (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:30; Hebrews 1:5).
Matthew builds Jesus' genealogy from the family lines of 1 Chronicles 2 and 3 (Matthew 1:1-17).

entries.when: Last centuries BC to first century AD
entries.what: Copies at Qumran by the Dead Sea: more manuscripts hold psalms than any other book. The Great Psalms Scroll orders the later psalms differently.
Rome removes Archelaus and sends him into exile. Judea is ruled by Roman governors from now on.
Judea comes under direct Roman rule. Quirinius, governor of Syria, takes a census (Acts 5:37).
Tiberius becomes emperor of Rome (until AD 37).
Tiberius becomes emperor of Rome (until AD 37).
Tiberius becomes emperor. Luke dates John's preaching by his fifteenth year (3:1).
A great earthquake strikes Sardis, Philadelphia and other cities of the region.
Antipas builds the city of Tiberias on the lake and names it for the emperor Tiberius. John calls the lake the Sea of Tiberias (6:1).
Pontius Pilate becomes the Roman governor of Judea (until about AD 36).
Pontius Pilate becomes the Roman governor of Judea (until about AD 36).
Pontius Pilate governs Judea. He tries Jesus and sends him to Herod (23:1-25).
Pontius Pilate governs Judea for Rome. He tries Jesus (chapters 18 and 19).
Pontius Pilate governs Judea. Peter reminds the crowd that Pilate had decided to release Jesus (3:13; 4:27).
John the Baptist preaches by the Jordan. Jesus is baptized and begins to preach in Galilee (Matthew 3 to 4).
John the Baptist preaches by the Jordan. Jesus is baptized and begins to teach in Galilee (Mark 1). Luke dates John's start to Tiberius's fifteenth year (Luke 3:1).
The fifteenth year of Tiberius on the usual count: John preaches and baptizes Jesus (3:1-22).
On the cross Jesus prays the first line of Psalm 22 (Mark 15:34); Luke records Psalm 31:5 as his last word (Luke 23:46).
In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16-21).
At his trial Jesus joins Daniel 7:13 to Psalm 110 to speak of himself (Mark 14:62).
The two dates most often proposed for Jesus' death and rising, as the notes on Acts give them. Seven weeks later, at Pentecost, Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32 (Acts 2:16-21).
In Acts, Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 before his death in the 30s (Acts 7), and later James quotes 9:11-12 at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15).
Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem at Passover and rises on the third day (Matthew 26 to 28). These are the two years most often proposed.
Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem at Passover and rises on the third day (Mark 14 to 16). These are the two years most often proposed.
The two dates most often proposed for the crucifixion.
The two dates most often proposed for the crucifixion.
The two dates most often proposed for Jesus' death and rising. Pentecost (2:1) comes seven weeks later.
The first believers in Jerusalem; Stephen's death; Saul meets the risen Jesus near Damascus (chapters 2 to 9).
The two dates most often proposed for the death and rising of Jesus in Jerusalem.
Paul, a zealous Pharisee who persecuted the church, meets the risen Christ near Damascus. He goes to Arabia and back to Damascus (1:15-17).
Paul goes up to Jerusalem and stays fifteen days with Peter, seeing also James, the Lord's brother (1:18-19).
Paul works in the regions of Syria and Cilicia, where his home town of Tarsus lay (1:21; Acts 9:30).
At Pentecost, Cretans are among the crowd in Jerusalem who hear the apostles (Acts 2:11).
The church meets in the Jerusalem house of Mary, John Mark's mother (Acts 12:12). Mark sets out with Paul and Barnabas and turns back (Acts 13:13).
The emperor Caligula orders his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple. The order is delayed, and dropped when he dies in AD 41.
Claudius is emperor. Acts names him for a famine (11:28) and for sending the Jews out of Rome (18:2).
Herod Agrippa I rules as king over Judea. He has James the brother of John put to death (12:1-2).
Claudius is emperor. Acts names him for sending the Jews out of Rome (Acts 18:2).
The reign of Claudius, when a famine strikes Judea and the church at Antioch sends help (Acts 11:28-30).
Agrippa dies suddenly at Caesarea, as Acts 12:20-23 and Josephus both tell, in the seventh year of Claudius.
Herod Agrippa I puts James the son of Zebedee to death (Acts 12:2).
The letter of James, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it, holds up Job's perseverance (James 5:11). Others date the letter later.
The letter of James, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it, quotes Proverbs 3:34 (James 4:6). Others date the letter later.
A severe famine in Judea, according to Josephus. The church in Antioch sends help by Barnabas and Saul (11:28-30).
The letter is written, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it. Some place it early, others in the late 50s or early 60s.
Barnabas and Paul start churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, in the southern part of the province of Galatia (Acts 13 and 14).
Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. The leaders give him the right hand of fellowship (2:1-10). Which visit in Acts this is, is debated.
The meeting in Jerusalem of Acts 15: Gentile believers need not be circumcised. Many think Galatians 2 tells of it; others think Galatians came first.
Paul writes Galatians. The earlier date goes with the south Galatian view; the later date with either view.
Paul and Barnabas start churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and suffer for it there (Acts 13 and 14; 2 Timothy 3:11).

entries.when: About AD 48 to 50, on many readings
entries.what: Titus goes up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas and is not made to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3).
Claudius expels Jews from Rome. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Claudius expels Jews from Rome, Suetonius says because of disturbances over ‘Chrestus’. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Claudius expels Jews from Rome. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Paul, Silas and Timothy come to Philippi. Lydia, a slave girl and a jailer; the church begins (Acts 16).
While Paul is in Thessalonica, the Philippians send him help more than once (4:16).
After being beaten and jailed in Philippi, Paul and Silas come to Thessalonica. The church begins, then they are sent away by night (Acts 17:1-10).
Paul goes on to Berea and Athens, and sends Timothy back from Athens to strengthen the church (3:1-2).
Paul, Silas and Timothy found the church in Thessalonica, and are driven out (Acts 17:1-10).
Paul meets Timothy at Lystra, and Timothy joins him (Acts 16:1-3).
Paul meets Timothy at Lystra, and Timothy joins him (Acts 16:1-3).
The emperor Claudius expels Jews from Rome. Some link the readers' early sufferings with this time (10:32-34).
The council in Jerusalem; James speaks for the church (Acts 15:13-21).
Silas, a leader in Jerusalem, is sent out with the council's letter and then travels with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40).
When Matthew was written. Some scholars argue for before AD 70; most place it between about 80 and 95.
Paul in Corinth for a year and a half, working with Aquila and Priscilla. The church begins (Acts 18:1-11).
Paul in Corinth for a year and a half with Silas and Timothy. The church begins (Acts 18:1-11).
Timothy rejoins Paul in Corinth with good news (3:6; Acts 18:5). Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, very likely his earliest surviving letter.
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians from Corinth.

entries.what: 2 Thessalonians, written from Corinth weeks or months after the first letter. This is the view of the church through history and of many scholars.
The date usually given by those who hold that Jude the brother of Jesus wrote it.
Gallio is proconsul of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul stands before him in Corinth (18:12).
Gallio is governor of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul is in Corinth for the first time, with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18).
Gallio is governor of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul is brought before him in Corinth (Acts 18:12).

Augustine of Hippo writes his long work on the Psalms, reading them as the prayer of Christ with his church.

entries.when: Early in Jehoiakim's reign, 609 or after
entries.what: Elders defend Jeremiah by quoting Micah 3:12 (Jeremiah 26:1, 18).
Bernard of Clairvaux preaches on the Song in the same tradition.
Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles begin to divide Ezra and Nehemiah into two books, as Christian Bibles long had.
John Calvin doubts that Peter wrote it but accepts it as Scripture.
Martin Luther lectures on Romans at Wittenberg. In 1545 he tells how Romans 1:17 opened to him.
Erasmus prints the Greek New Testament without those words, then adds them in his third edition.
Luther's preface ranks James below the letters he thought showed Christ most clearly.
William Tyndale coins the English word ‘scapegoat’ for the goat of chapter 16.
A commentary from Martin Luther's lectures on Galatians is published. He called it the letter he loved most.
John Bunyan, in Grace Abounding, praises Luther's Galatians as most fit for a wounded conscience.
The name ‘Pastoral Letters’ comes into use for 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus.
A three-character reading is first proposed: the woman, her shepherd lover and Solomon as a rival. It becomes popular in the nineteenth.
At a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, John Wesley hears Luther's preface to Romans read and feels his ‘heart strangely warmed’.
The French doctor Jean Astruc notices that parts of Genesis call God ‘God’ and others ‘the LORD’, and suggests Moses used sources.
Robert Lowth publishes his Oxford lectures on Hebrew poetry, describing the paired lines called parallelism.
Most interpreters come to read the Song first as poetry of human love; many hold that reading together with the older one.
W. M. L. de Wette argues that the scroll found under Josiah was an early form of Deuteronomy.
In the United States, the Fugitive Slave Act. Defenders of slavery cite Philemon in its support; abolitionists answer from verse 16.
The spiritual Go Down, Moses is first published, from the singing of escaped slaves.
Charles Warren finds a shaft in Jerusalem, long linked with the water shaft of 5:8. Later excavations suggest it was not accessible in David's time.
George Smith reads his translation of the Gilgamesh flood tablet in London (1872) and publishes Enuma Elish (1876).
A Norwegian physician identifies the bacterium of the disease now called leprosy. Its marks are not those of the skin disease in Leviticus 13.
August Klostermann gives chapters 17 to 26 the name the Holiness Code.
The Cyrus Cylinder is found in the ruins of Babylon. It is now in the British Museum.
Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena gives the four-source theory of the Torah its classic form.
Édouard Naville excavates Tell el-Maskhuta in the valley east of the Delta and takes it to be Pithom.
Bernhard Duhm proposes separating chapters 56 to 66, after Döderlein and Eichhorn had separated 40 to 66 in the late eighteenth century.
Karl Barth's commentary on Romans appears (printed at the end of 1918), rewritten in a second edition in 1922.
Leonhard Rost argues for an older story of the ark inside the book.
The scrap P52, with words from John 18, is bought in Egypt and then published by C. H. Roberts.
Thomas Chisholm writes a hymn that takes its name from ‘great is Your faithfulness’ (3:23).
Adolf Erman shows that Proverbs 22:17 to 23:11 closely parallels the Instruction of Amenemope.
Leonhard Rost argues that 2 Samuel 9 to 20 and 1 Kings 1 and 2 form one story of the succession to David's throne.
John Garstang, Kathleen Kenyon and Bryant Wood date the fall of Jericho differently. The question is still argued.
Hermann Gunkel's Introduction to the Psalms, finished by Joachim Begrich after Gunkel's death, sorts the psalms into kinds.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer publishes a short book on the Psalms as the prayer book of the Bible.

George Mendenhall proposes that elef in the census lists means a military unit, not a thousand.
C. S. Lewis publishes Reflections on the Psalms, facing the cursing psalms honestly.
Kathleen Kenyon finds collapsed terraces on the eastern slope of the City of David, and Nahman Avigad uncovers a massive wall he names the Broad Wall after 3:8.
